q.intro.text: A dilation has a center O and a scale factor k equals two. Dilate triangle ABC about O.

q.ask.text: Where does the corner C one, four land? Pick a point, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the board writes it down.

e.s1.text: A dilation pushes every point straight away from the center. Draw a ray from O through each corner: each image lands on its own ray.

e.s2.text: k equals two means twice as far from O. O to C is one amber bar; O to C prime is two of them. So C one, four lands on C prime two, eight.

e.s3.text: Do the same for A and B, and join the image. With the center at the origin, every coordinate doubles: x, y goes to two x, two y.

e.s4.text: Check what stays. The right angle is still a right angle, and A, B, C still goes counterclockwise. Every side doubled: eight divided by four equals four divided by two equals two.

e.why.text: Quick check: why is point one, negative one, five, not the image of C?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. The center is O, so C prime must be on ray OC. Point one was pushed out from the middle of the triangle instead.

e.w-add.text: Adding two to each coordinate gives three, six, point three. A dilation multiplies the distance from O by two; it does not add two.

e.w-mid.text: The center is whatever the problem says: here, O. The middle of the triangle is a different center, and it gives a different image.

t.intro.text: Your turn. Dilate triangle PQR about O with k equals one half. The rays and the image of P are done for you.

t.p.text: P negative six, four is six left and four up from O. Half as far: P prime negative three, two.

t.q-ask.text: Your step: where does Q negative two, four land?

t.q-ok.text: Yes: half of negative two, four is negative one, two. Q prime is on ray OQ, half as far from O.

t.q-big.text: That doubled it. k equals one half is less than one, so the image comes closer to O.

t.q-sign.text: Right size, wrong sign. Q is left of O, so Q prime is left of O too: half of negative two is negative one.

t.q-one.text: Halve both coordinates, not just one.

t.q-same.text: That is Q itself. Here Q moves halfway toward O.

t.q-no.text: Count from O to Q: two left and four up. Take half of each.

t.len-ask.text: PR is six units long. How long is P prime R prime?

t.len-ok.text: Yes: one half times six equals three.

t.len-big.text: Twelve is six times two. The image is smaller: one half times six.

t.len-same.text: Only k equals one keeps lengths. Here every length is halved.

t.len-sub.text: The scale factor multiplies: one half times six, not six minus one half.

t.len-no.text: Multiply the length by the scale factor, one half.

t.true-ask.text: Which is true for triangle P prime Q prime R prime?

t.true-ok.text: Right: a dilation multiplies every length by k and keeps every angle.

t.true-add.text: The sides are multiplied by one half, not shortened by two: the six became three, the four became two.

t.true-ang.text: Angles are not halved: the right angle at P prime is still ninety degrees.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked point two, and you were right: C prime is on ray OC, twice as far from O.

t.cb-mid.text: At the start you picked point one. That grows the triangle from its own middle. The center was O, so every image lies on a ray from O.

t.cb-add.text: At the start you picked point three. That adds two to each coordinate. A dilation multiplies the distance from the center instead.

t.cb-none.text: Every image lands on its ray from the center, k times as far away.

p.intro.text: Riley has two rectangles: R is six by four and S is nine by five. Riley says: “Both have four right angles, so R and S are similar.”

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each “because” with the reason that makes the line true.

p.build-test.text: Let’s test it. Fill each “because” with the reason that makes the line true, and see where it leads.

p.c1.text: Right. A dilation stretches every side by the same k, and rigid motions never change a length.

p.c2.text: Right. Three halves times six equals nine, but three halves times four equals six, and S is only five tall: a strip is left over.

p.c3.text: Right. Matching angles are not enough for four-sided shapes. The sides have to share one ratio too.

p.no-angles.text: That is Riley’s mistake. A long thin rectangle and a square both have four right angles, but they are not the same shape.

p.no-diff.text: Similar figures are compared by dividing, not subtracting: the question is whether one k works for every side.

p.no-one.text: One pair of sides is never enough. The short sides must give the same k as the long sides.

p.x-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That’s a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the picture backs every one. R and S are not similar.
